newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. backing boosts Canadian plan to ban landmines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. backing boosts Canadian plan to ban landmines.

text.p: President Clinton's decision on Monday to support Canada's initiative for a global ban on landmines could give the process a boost, but full agreement is still far from certain, officials and analysts said.

"I think the American support will give it momentum," Edward McWhinney, parliamentary secretary to Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, told Reuters. "It's good news for Canada and the world community."

Clinton, who is vacationing on the Massachusetts island of Martha's Vineyard, on Monday gave his backing to the so-called Ottawa Process to ban the use, export, production and stockpiling of landmines after it became clear that a U.N. conference in Geneva was unlikely to produce a breakthrough on the ban.
Clinton had rejected the Canadian initiative in January after concluding it left little room for exceptions sought by U.S. military commanders.
But the White House changed its mind after concluding there had been little progess on controlling landmines through the U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.

"The United States is committed to pursuing the most promising opportunities for ending the use of anti-personnel landmines, which every year cause enormous suffering around the world," the White House said in a statement. U.S. officials said Washington was not abandoning the Geneva talks, but would shift some of its efforts to the Ottawa Process.
Antipersonnel landmines, designed to maim, claim a new victim every 22 minutes, Canadian officials estimate. Most of the victims are women and children in war-torn areas.
More than 50 countries have said they support the Ottawa Process. Representatives will gather in Oslo in two weeks to negotiate a draft treaty to be signed in Ottawa in December.
Australia, Argentina and Chile gave their backing to the Ottawa Process last week. Now, with the United States on side, other key countries will have to take notice, analysts said.

"To get the Americans inside the tent is vital," military analyst Alex Morrison, president of Canada's Pearson Peacekeeping Centre, told Reuters. "Now that they're there, it will influence other countries, and other countries will want to join on."

Russia, China, India and Pakistan -- key landmine producers -- have not backed the process, prompting other countries to hold back their support too. While U.S. support for the ban may not prompt Russia and China to back the Ottawa Process, it may encourage them to reconsider their landmine policies, Morrison said.
"It will certainly influence the decision-making processes in China and Russia," he said. "No country wants to be left out in the cold."
Even so, the American presence at the negotiating table could force Canada to compromise, he said.

The United States faces pressure from the Joint Chiefs of Staff who argue they should be able to use so-called "smart mines" that will self-destruct. Canada and other critics contend that those mines are too unreliable.
And U.S. State Department spokesman James Rubin said on Monday that the United States wants a "geographic exception" for its land mines on the Korean peninsula.
"North Korea forces are on a high state of alert and there is always the risk of an attack from North Korea," Rubin said in Washington.
But the Canadian government was not enthusiastic about such exceptions, emphasizing that the process aims for a total worldwide ban of landmines.
"Our policy remains the same," Foreign Affairs spokesman Rodney Moore said in a phone interview. "We'll be seeking a treaty which establishes a clear and unambiguous ban."
